Subject: Pricing metrics: tokens vs characters vs requests - quick clarification

Thanks for the demo this morning. Quick follow-up - we have some internal confusion on how we should estimate costs for our ingest-heavy flows.

Specifically:
- Are billed units 'tokens' or 'characters'?
- How does prompt caching affect billing - if we cache prompts, will the customer still be billed for the cached input tokens on subsequent requests?
- Does Redwood bill per request in addition to token usage (we have many small requests)?

Our SRE team asked for a target $/1M tokens to plug into forecasts. Can you confirm the unit economics we should model (including any per-request overhead)?

Thanks,
Sam

Hey Sam - thanks for the great questions and for having us today. Below is a concise breakdown to help with forecasting; I've also attached a short pricing summary and a spreadsheet example tailored to ingest-heavy workloads.

1) Billed units = tokens (not characters).
   - Characters are an imperfect proxy; tokenization varies by language and punctuation. We recommend modeling using tokens.

2) Prompt caching vs billed tokens:
   - Billing is based on actual tokens processed by the model for each request.
   - If you cache a prompt server-side and send a much smaller delta (e.g., just a context ID) to Redwood, you will only be billed for the tokens actually sent and generated.
   - However, our hosted API charges based on the request payload we receive. So internal caching that reduces request token size reduces billed tokens.

3) Per-request overhead:
   - There is no separate per-request "token" fee. Billing = input_tokens + output_tokens.
   - For very high QPS with many tiny requests, networking and throughput efficiency matter; Redwood Optimize can suggest batching or prefix caching to lower unit cost.
   - For Dedicated customers we offer discounts and commit pricing that effectively reduces the $/1M tokens.

4) Target $/1M tokens:
   - For a hosted run-rate forecast, a conservative public estimate is $X per 1M tokens (see attached summary for current list rates and typical discounts).
   - With batching/prompt caching and a Dedicated commitment, effective $/1M can be materially lower.

Next steps I propose:
- I attached a quick spreadsheet (acme_multiproduct_estimate.xlsx) - fill in your estimated monthly token volumes (ingest + generation) and we can run the numbers.
- If helpful, Aditya can run a micro-sim of your sample traffic (anonymized) to show token breakdown and cost with/without batching.

Cc'ing Aditya for the micro-sim and Dev for any questions on request-level instrumentation.

Best,

Hi Sam - quick note from the infra side. A couple of practical clarifications that often help teams forecast more accurately:

- Token counts: when you run our tokenizer on a typical paragraph, expect ~0.7-1.2 tokens per word depending on language and punctuation. We can share a small script to estimate tokens from your sample docs.

- Prompt caching pattern: two common approaches:
  1) Client-side composition: you store the full prompt server-side and only send a short identifier; Redwood will see a small token count per request (low cost).
  2) Server-side expansion: you expand the prompt and send the full prompt each request - you'll be billed for those tokens each time.

- Batching: for many small requests, queueing a short window (50-200ms) to batch requests can reduce overall compute and amortize overhead - can cut $/1M effective cost by ~10-30% depending on traffic shape.

If you can drop a 24-48 hour sample of 1000 typical requests (anonymized), I'll run tokenization and show projected billed tokens with and without caching/batching.

Cheers,
